match.reason: The closest bank point, pe-levers-body, only introduces the basic lever parts (axis, force, load) at Units 1 and 2 depth, while the new point teaches third-class levers and the force-for-speed trade-off in mechanical advantage, which is a different idea and a deeper step.

draft.title: Levers in the body
card: A lever is a rigid bar that turns around a fixed point. In the body, a bone is the bar, a joint is the axis, and a muscle pulls to apply the force against a resistance, such as a weight or the limb itself.
First class
the axis sits between the force and the resistance, like a seesaw. Nodding the head is an example.
Second class

the resistance sits between the axis and the force, like a wheelbarrow. Rising onto the toes is an example. The force arm (axis to force) is longer than the resistance arm (axis to resistance), so less force is needed.
Third class

the force sits between the axis and the resistance. Bending the elbow to lift a weight is an example. The force arm is shorter than the resistance arm, so more force is needed, but the load moves faster through a larger range. Most body movements use this type.
draft.remember: Most body levers are third class: a short force arm needs more muscle force but gives speed.

a.q: In a bicep curl, the biceps pulls on the forearm between the elbow and the hand holding the weight. Which class of lever is this?
opts: Third class: the force is in the middle
Second class: the resistance is in the middle
First class: the axis is in the middle
Second class: the force is in the middle
a.why: The elbow is the axis, the biceps pull is the force, and the weight in the hand is the resistance. The force lies between the other two, so it is third class. Second class has the resistance in the middle, which is not the case here.
a.clue: Find which of the three parts sits in the middle.

b.q: Jess swings a hockey stick using a third-class lever action at her elbow. Compared with a lever whose force arm is longer than its resistance arm, what does her lever give her?
opts: Faster hand movement, but more muscle force needed
Greater force at the hand, but a slower movement
Less muscle force needed, and a faster movement
More muscle force needed, and a slower movement
b.why: In a third-class lever the force acts close to the axis, so the force arm is short and the resistance arm is long. The muscle must pull harder to move the load, but the hand moves quickly through a large range. Greater force with less speed describes a lever with a longer force arm.
b.clue: The force acts close to the joint, while the load is far away.

a.best: Third class: the force is in the middle

b.best: Faster hand movement, but more muscle force needed

problems.detail: The stem calls the elbow action in a hockey swing a third-class lever. Elbow extension in a swing is driven by the triceps, which is the standard first-class lever example, so this claim is doubtful. An action that is clearly third class, such as elbow flexion, would avoid teaching a questionable classification.

check.summary: The card, the remember line and question a are accurate. Question b's hockey example is doubtful, because elbow extension during a swing is usually a first-class (triceps) lever, not third class.
